common_name: Texas Scarlet Flowering Quince (Compact Red-Orange Flowering Quince)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in any well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Texas Scarlet's compact, low-mounding habit fits foundation plantings and smaller beds where the larger straight species would need frequent hard pruning to control.

directions: Texas Scarlet is a compact, spreading flowering quince selection covering itself in brilliant red-orange flowers directly on the bare, twiggy stems in late winter and very early spring, well before the leaves emerge, making it one of the earliest color displays of the gardening year. Its low, mounding habit stays well under 4 feet, more manageable than many older flowering quince cultivars, and small yellow-green, quince-scented fruit follows the bloom, edible when cooked into jelly or preserves though rarely eaten raw. Extremely adaptable to poor, clay, sandy, or alkaline soil once established and quite drought-tolerant, it blooms on old wood, so prune only immediately after flowering to avoid removing next year's buds.

common_name: Cameo Flowering Quince (Double Peach-Pink Flowering Quince)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in any well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Cameo's compact, thornless-to-nearly-thornless habit and softer flower color make it a good choice for a foundation planting near a walkway.

directions: Cameo carries fully double, soft peachy-pink flowers, a gentler pastel departure from the hot reds and oranges typical of most flowering quince cultivars, opening directly on the bare stems in late winter into early spring ahead of the foliage. Its compact, rounded, largely thornless growth habit makes it easier to work around than older, thornier quince cultivars, and small yellow-green fruit follows the bloom, usable for jelly and preserves though not typically eaten fresh. Extremely tolerant of poor, clay, sandy, or alkaline soil once established, it blooms on old wood, so prune only right after flowering to avoid cutting off next season's flower buds.

common_name: Toyo Nishiki Flowering Quince (Multicolor Pink-White-Red Flowering Quince)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in any well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Toyo Nishiki blooms on old wood, so prune, if needed, only immediately after flowering to avoid removing next year's buds.

directions: Toyo Nishiki is a classic flowering quince cultivar famous for producing white, pink, and red flowers all at once on the same branch, and sometimes even within a single blossom, an unpredictable multicolor mix that makes each spring's bloom slightly different from the last. It flowers directly on the bare, thorny stems in late winter into early spring ahead of the foliage, forming a large, vigorous, arching shrub, and small yellow-green, quince-scented fruit follows the bloom, valued for jelly and preserves rather than fresh eating. Highly adaptable to poor, clay, sandy, or alkaline soil once established and notably drought-tolerant, it makes an effective thorny barrier hedge in addition to its ornamental value.

common_name: Belle Etoile Mock Orange (Purple-Blotched Fragrant Mock Orange)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Belle Etoile is a classic French Lemoine hybrid grown for its intensely fragrant, distinctively marked flowers rather than the plainer solid-white blooms of most mock orange selections.

directions: Belle Etoile is a French-bred mock orange prized for single, pure-white, four-petaled flowers each marked at the center with a distinctive maroon-purple blotch, a striking contrast on a plant otherwise similar to standard mock orange. The flowers open in a heavy late-spring flush and carry an intense, sweet orange-blossom fragrance that can perfume an entire garden corner, borne on a medium-sized, rounded, arching shrub. Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and prune immediately after flowering to shape, since Belle Etoile blooms on old wood and later pruning removes the following year's fragrant display.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Show Off requires full sun for the heaviest flower coverage, and its more compact size than older forsythia cultivars needs less pruning to control.

directions: Show Off is a compact forsythia bred to flower along the entire length of every branch, from the base to the tip, rather than mainly at the branch tips as in older cultivars, producing an unusually dense, solid mass of golden-yellow flowers in late winter before the leaves emerge. Its smaller mature size, roughly half that of standard border forsythia, fits foundation plantings and smaller gardens without the annual hard pruning that larger forsythia cultivars need to stay in bounds. Like all forsythia, flower bud hardiness is the limiting factor outside its ideal cold-winter range — flower buds need a period of cold dormancy and can be damaged by extended warm spells in mild winters, so bloom performance in zone 9 varies from year to year depending on winter chill.
